title: Coral and the Smile
premise: Beatrix Amberdale, a nonbinary property surveyor who has spent seven years keeping their head down in the decaying seaside town of Gullmere, is sent to appraise Holloway House—a Victorian pile whose rooms rearrange themselves and whose walls hum a lullaby no one wrote. When Beatrix's sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions they never asked aloud, they learn the house is fed by a chorus of vanished residents, each swallowed for singing along to the song's final verse. Digging into Gullmere's records, Beatrix uncovers that the town's founding families have been feeding people to the house for generations in exchange for prosperity—and that their own late mother was one of its keepers. In the climax, Beatrix refuses to sing the last verse alone, instead teaching it back to the house itself, turning the hunger inward; the founding families' heirs are claimed by what they raised, the trapped voices are freed, and Beatrix—no longer invisible—chooses to stay in Gullmere as the keeper of an empty house, finally part of a found family of survivors.
about_author: M. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties along the English coast before turning to fiction. They write horror about houses, inheritance, and the quiet violence of being overlooked.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Arriving at Holloway House with a clipboard and seven years of practiced invisibility, Beatrix measures rooms that don't match their own measurements. The emotional beat is wary professionalism cracking into unease as the tape measure returns different numbers on the second pass.

chapters.title: Explanations
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Scratches above the ceiling, a smell of brine, doors ajar that were locked—Beatrix catalogs rational causes in their surveyor's notebook. The beat is self-soothing routine, showing how seven years of denial has become a discipline.

chapters.title: The Hum
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At dusk the walls begin humming a tune Beatrix almost recognizes, something like a lullaby half-remembered from childhood. They leave without finishing the appraisal but accept the return appointment anyway. The beat is the first conscious choice to go back.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ferrow's Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The estate agent, Mrs. Ferrow, hands over deeds going back to 1841 and warns Beatrix, oddly, not to work past sundown. A name in the ledger—Amberdale—stops Beatrix cold. The beat is the first crack in the family myth of their mother's respectable death.

chapters.title: Recorders Running
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Unable to sleep, Beatrix sets their old voice recorder beside the bed out of surveyor's habit: document everything. The chapter ends with them waking to eight hours of footage they're afraid to play. The beat is dread deferred.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The recording captures Beatrix asleep asking questions—who are you, what do you want—and a second voice, wet and patient, answering. One answer is a name: 'Keeper.' The beat is terror fused with a horrible sense of being expected.

chapters.title: Gullmere's Welcome
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Odile Vann, a diner cook and unofficial archivist of the town's poor. She notices Beatrix eating alone three nights running and sits down uninvited. The beat is gruff kindness offered to someone clearly haunted.

chapters.title: The Drowned Census
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile shows Beatrix her private project: forty years of missing persons, all appraisers, caretakers, and drifters—people nobody would miss. Every disappearance clusters around property transfers of Holloway House. The beat is the comfort of pattern, and its horror.

chapters.title: Verse One
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Back in the house, Beatrix hums the first line of the lullaby experimentally; the walls fall silent, listening. That night the recorder catches the second voice saying 'again.' The beat is the intoxicating, dangerous feeling of being heard.

chapters.title: Mother's Box
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Following the ledger's Amberdale entry, Beatrix opens a storage unit their mother paid for until her death. Inside: sheet music titled 'The Keeper's Verse,' four verses, the last torn out. The beat is grief weaponized into purpose.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile names the five dynasties—the Vanns among them once—who still own most of Gullmere and meet quarterly at the marina. Her estranged brother Rennick is their lawyer. The beat is Odile's shame at her own bloodline exposed.

chapters.title: Questions at Night
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix begins sleeping in the house deliberately, asking the second voice questions on purpose. It tells them: 'We sang. We stayed. You will too.' The voices give fragments of names. The beat is empathy blooming toward the trapped.

chapters.title: Rennick Vann
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile confronts Rennick at his office; he deflects with charm, then quietly threatens her lease. She realizes he knows exactly what the house is. The beat is rage at power that smiles while it feeds.

chapters.title: The Surveyor Before
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix tracks down the family of Danny Osei, an appraiser missing since 2019, and finds his last report: measurements that grow, a note reading 'it appraises back.' His mother begs Beatrix to drop it. The beat is guilt—Beatrix could still walk away.

chapters.title: Verse Two
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Singing the second verse makes the house warm, almost kind—rooms tidy themselves, the brine smell turns to bread. Beatrix understands the trap: the house rewards you for singing. The beat is temptation dressed as belonging.

chapters.title: Found Family, Forming
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Odile starts hosting Sunday dinners for the houseless and half-lost of Gullmere; Beatrix attends, awkward, then returns. The beat is the slow, unfamiliar warmth of being included.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. In the house's sealed nursery, behind wallpaper, Beatrix finds the fourth verse penciled on plaster: instructions for feeding the house a singer so it 'keeps' you forever. The beat is revulsion—the lullaby is a recipe.

chapters.title: What the Heirs Know
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile infiltrates the marina meeting disguised as catering staff and hears the heirs discuss the house's 'appetite' and the coming 'vacancy'—a keeper must be bound before winter or the town's fortunes fail. The beat is cold clarity about the machinery of Gullmere.

chapters.title: They Know Your Name
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Mrs. Ferrow delivers new paperwork listing Beatrix as 'resident caretaker, per family instruction.' Someone has forged their signature beautifully. The beat is the vertigo of realizing invisibility was always someone else's arrangement.

chapters.title: The Second Voice's Story
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The voice identifies herself: Elowen Pryce, taken in 1953, the last keeper who refused to finish the verse. She warns: the house cannot be burned, sold, or starved—only sung against. The beat is alliance across death.

chapters.title: Midnight Audit
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix does what they do best: a full structural audit of the house, mapping where the voices pool strongest—an old cistern beneath the kitchen. The beat is competence as courage; fear channeled into method.

chapters.title: Odile Disappears
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Odile misses Sunday dinner. Her apartment is scrubbed, her census archive gone. Rennick's card lies on her table like a tip. The beat is panic curdling into resolve—Beatrix will not be invisible to this.

chapters.title: The Cistern
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Descending into the cistern, Beatrix finds the missing: not bodies but presences, dozens, humming in the dark water's reflection. Odile's voice is newly among them, still fighting the song. The beat is horror and hope tangled.

chapters.title: Bargaining with Brine
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix offers the house a trade—themselves for Odile. The house counters: sing all four verses willingly and both may stay, comfortable, forever. The word 'comfortable' is the threat. The beat is temptation at its most surgical.

chapters.title: Elowen's Refusal
chapters.summary: Elowen's POV (through the recorder). A 1953 recording surfaces in the house's own wiring: Elowen explaining why she stopped—the verse doesn't bind the singer to the house, it binds the house to the singer. Whoever finishes it owns the hunger. The beat is revelation reframing everything.

chapters.title: The Heirs' Winter
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, from inside. Held in the house's dream-space, Odile watches the heirs arrive to consecrate a new keeper and recognizes the ceremony from childhood stories her grandmother sang. The beat is Odile reclaiming her heritage as knowledge instead of complicity.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. With Elowen coaching through the walls, Beatrix memorizes the fourth verse—not to sing it, but to know it better than the house does. The beat is preparation as defiance; mastery over the thing meant to master them.

chapters.title: Danny's Tape
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Danny Osei's old recorder, hidden in the attic, holds his final hours: he nearly finished the verse alone and the house nearly took him whole. His error was singing solo. The beat is the plan crystallizing: no one sings alone.

chapters.title: Consecration Eve
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The heirs gather at Holloway House with contracts and candles; Beatrix hides in the cistern with Odile's coat, planning. The beat is the hush before violence, every player in position.

chapters.title: The Chorus Wakes
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The heirs force the ceremony early, using Beatrix's forged residency as consent. The house begins pulling all the voices upward to fuel the binding. The beat is betrayal made architectural.

chapters.title: Singing Against
chapters.summary: Climax begins. Beatrix steps into the parlor and sings verses one through three loudly, claiming the song, then offers the fourth—but changes the words, addressing the house itself as the singer. The beat is audacity: turning the recipe back on the chef.

chapters.title: What Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Climax. The house, bound by its own verse, begins auditing its owners—measuring the heirs against what they've fed it. Rooms close on the Vanns, the Ferrows, the founding names. Rennick tries to flee and is appraised wanting. The beat is justice outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: Elowen's Last Note
chapters.summary: Climax. Elowen spends seventy years of held breath to hold the final chord steady while Beatrix and the freed voices carry the changed verse. She thins to a smell of rain and is gone, smiling. The beat is sacrifice transfigured into release.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Measured
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Dawn. The house stands empty and ordinary, every room exactly the size it should be. The heirs' fortunes collapse overnight; Gullmere wakes poorer and lighter. The beat is exhausted, disbelieving calm.

chapters.title: Odile, Returned
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile wakes on the kitchen floor with salt in her hair and no memory of the cistern, holding her grandmother's recipe box the house somehow returned. The beat is survival's disorientation, and gratitude she can't yet say aloud.

chapters.title: The Town Learns
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Fragments spread—Danny Osei's mother gets her son's recorder back with his voice on it saying goodbye. Some townsfolk thank Beatrix; some cross the street. The beat is the loneliness of truth-telling, softened by those who believe.

chapters.title: Sunday Dinner
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Odile reopens her Sundays; Beatrix cooks badly and is teased for it. Danny's mother comes. The found family assembles itself without anyone naming it. The beat is belonging chosen, not sung for.

chapters.title: Keeper of an Empty House
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Beatrix signs the deed—legally this time—as caretaker of Holloway House, now silent, kept as a memorial with the names of the taken carved in the stairwell. The beat is stewardship replacing escape.

chapters.title: The Song's End
chapters.summary: Final chapter, dual POV. On the anniversary, Beatrix and Odile walk the house together; in the cistern, faintly, the voices sound like they're resting rather than waiting. Beatrix hums only the first verse, and nothing answers—which is its own kind of peace. The beat is closure: the noise finally has an explanation, and it's love.
